title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6
summary: Defines the changes to DNS to support IPv6 hosts. It adds the AAAA resource record type for storing an IPv6 address, a domain for looking up names from IPv6 addresses, and updated definitions of existing query types that return addresses. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3596 adds DNS rules for IPv6 addresses. It defines a record that stores an IPv6 address, a domain for looking up names from addresses, and additional address information for certain DNS responses.

questions: how do i do an ipv6 reverse dns lookup
subtitle: The AAAA record and IP6.ARPA domain let DNS store IPv6 addresses and look them up by address.

tldr.problem: Existing DNS address support was designed around IPv4 addresses, so DNS needed a way to store IPv6 addresses and look up names from those addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the AAAA record for one IPv6 address, the IP6.ARPA domain for address-based lookups, and changes additional-section processing for NS, SRV and MX queries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3596 is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1886 and RFC 3152, combining their IPv6 DNS extensions and replacing IP6.INT with IP6.ARPA.

facts.label: Updated query types
facts.value: NS, SRV and MX additional processing

today: RFC 3596 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1886 and RFC 3152. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 3596.

sections.title: The IPv6 DNS Extensions
sections.content:
Applications had assumed that DNS address queries returned 32-bit IPv4 addresses, making it difficult to add IPv6 addresses to the existing approach. RFC 3596 defines three extensions: a record type that maps a name to an IPv6 address, a domain for lookups based on an IPv6 address, and changes to existing queries that add address records to responses.

The RFC is designed to work with existing software and keeps IPv4 support. The IP version used to carry a query is independent of the IP version of the records it requests.

RFC 3596 combines RFC 1886 and changes made by RFC 3152. Its main change from those documents is use of IP6.ARPA in place of IP6.INT.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS can use IPv4 transport to ask for IPv6 records, or IPv6 transport to ask for IPv4 records. The extensions keep the existing IPv4 support while adding IPv6 address records and lookups.

sections.title: The AAAA Record and Query
sections.content:
The AAAA resource record stores one IPv6 address in the Internet class. Its DNS type value is 28. The record data holds the 128-bit address in network byte order, with the high-order byte first.

A host with more than one IPv6 address has more than one AAAA record. An AAAA query returns all associated AAAA records in the answer section of the response.

An AAAA query does not trigger additional-section processing. In a master database file, the record's text form is the IPv6 address notation defined by the cited IPv6 addressing specification.
sections.plainLanguage: An AAAA record stores one IPv6 address for a name. If the name has several IPv6 addresses, DNS can return several AAAA records.

sections.title: Reverse Lookups with IP6.ARPA
sections.content:
The IP6.ARPA domain lets a client look up a record using an IPv6 address. Its intended use is mapping an address to a host name, though the RFC allows other purposes.

To form a name, write each four-bit part of the address as a hexadecimal digit, separate the digits with dots and reverse their order. Append .IP6.ARPA. The example in the RFC starts with address 4321:0:1:2:3:4:567:89ab and shows the corresponding reversed sequence of digits.

The reversed order begins with the lowest-order digit of the address. Each digit is a separate DNS label.
sections.plainLanguage: For a reverse lookup, write the IPv6 address as hexadecimal digits in reverse order, with dots between them. Add the IP6.ARPA ending to make the DNS name.

sections.title: Additional Addresses in DNS Responses
sections.content:
Three existing query types already perform additional-section processing for IPv4 A records: name server (NS), service location (SRV) and mail exchange (MX). RFC 3596 requires this processing to include both A and AAAA records.

When responding to one of these queries, a name server must add relevant IPv4 and IPv6 addresses available locally to the additional section. This can provide address records for names mentioned in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: NS, SRV and MX responses can include relevant IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in their additional section. This gives the requester address information for the names in the response.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says DNS information should be treated as unsafe unless the DNS Security Extensions or TSIG techniques it cites are used. Defining AAAA and IP6.ARPA does not change how those techniques work.

The document is not believed to create new security problems or solve existing ones. It also says there are no IANA assignments to perform.
sections.plainLanguage: These DNS extensions do not change how DNS security techniques work. The RFC says DNS answers still need those techniques when they must be trusted.

sections.title: Changes from the Earlier IPv6 DNS Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3596 brings together RFC 1886 and the changes made to it by RFC 3152, and obsoletes both. It replaces the IP6.INT reverse-lookup domain with IP6.ARPA.

Other listed changes include adding SRV queries to the additional-section rules, adding security and IANA considerations, and updating references and document structure.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC combines two earlier documents about IPv6 in DNS. Its main protocol change is using IP6.ARPA instead of IP6.INT for reverse lookups.

items.title: AAAA record
items.text: Stores one IPv6 address for a name.

items.title: IP6.ARPA
items.text: Supports queries based on an IPv6 address.

items.title: Additional-section processing
items.text: NS, SRV and MX responses add relevant A and AAAA records.
